The parent issue with description is #2690 

Proposed level changes for requirement in chapter "V5 Encoding and Sanitization"

Full list of requirements for the chapter is listed here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x13-V5-Encoding-Sanitization.md

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **5.2.2** | [MODIFIED] Verify that data being passed to a potentially dangerous context is sanitized beforehand to enforce safety measures, such as only allowing characters which are safe for this context and trimming input which is too long. | 1 > 2 |
| **5.2.3** | Verify that the application sanitizes user input before passing to mail systems to protect against SMTP or IMAP injection. | 1 > 3 |
| **5.2.5** | [MODIFIED] Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not allowing templates to be built based on untrusted input. Where there is no alternative, any untrusted input being included dynamically during template creation must be sanitized or strictly validated. | 1 > 2 |
| **5.2.6** | [MODIFIED] Verify that the application protects against Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks, by validating untrusted data against an allowlist of protocols, domains, paths and ports and sanitizing potentially dangerous characters before using the data to call another service. | 1 > 2 |
| **5.2.7** | [MODIFIED] Verify that user-supplied Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) scriptable content is validated or sanitized to contain only tags and attributes (such as draw graphics) that are safe for the application, e.g., do not contain scripts and foreignObject. | 1 > 2 |
| **5.2.8** | Verify that the application sanitizes, disables, or sandboxes user-supplied scriptable or expression template language content, such as Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets, BBCode, or similar. | 1 > 2 |
| **5.2.9** | [ADDED] Verify that the application uses slashes to correctly escape special characters being used in regular expressions to ensure they are not misinterpreted as control characters. | 1 > 2 |
| **5.2.10** | [ADDED] Verify that regular expressions are free from elements causing exponential backtracking, and ensure untrusted input is sanitized to mitigate ReDoS or Runaway Regex attacks. | 1 > 3 |
| **5.2.11** | [ADDED] Verify that the application appropriately sanitizes untrusted input before use in Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) queries and that JNDI is configured as securely as possible to prevent JNDI injection attacks. | 1 > 3 |
| **5.2.12** | [ADDED] Verify that the application sanitizes content before it is sent to memcache to prevent injection attacks. | 2 > 3 |
| **5.3.7** | Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities, or that specific security controls to prevent LDAP injection have been implemented. | 1 > 3 |
| **5.3.10** | [MODIFIED] Verify that the application is protected against XPath injection attacks by using query parameterization or precompiled queries. | 1 > 3 |
| **5.3.11** | [ADDED] Verify that the application is protected against CSV and Formula Injection. The application should follow the escaping rules defined in RFC4180 2.6 and 2.7 when exporting CSV files. The application should escape special characters including '=', '+', '-', '@' '\t' (tab) and '\00' (null character) using a single quote, if they are the first character in a field, when exporting CSV files and other spreadsheet formats such as xls, xlsx, odf. | 1 > 3 |
| **5.3.12** | [ADDED] Verify that LaTeX processors are configured securely (such as not using the "--shell-escape" flag) and an allowlist of commands is used to prevent LaTeX injection attacks. | 2 > 3 |
| **5.5.3** | [MODIFIED, MERGED FROM 1.5.2] Verify that deserialization with untrusted clients enforces safe input handling, such as using an allowlist of object types or restricting client-defined object types, to prevent deserialization attacks. Deserialization mechanisms that are explicitly defined as insecure (such as BinaryFormatter) must not be used with untrusted input. | 1 > 2 |
| **5.5.5** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 13.1.1, LEVEL L1 > L2] Verify that different parsers used in the application for the same data type (e.g., JSON parsers, XML parsers, URL parsers), perform parsing in a consistent way and use the same character encoding mechanism to avoid issues such as JSON Interoperability vulnerabilities or different URI or file parsing behavior being exploited in Remote File Inclusion (RFI) or Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks. | 2 > 3 |
| **5.6.1** | [ADDED] Verify that input is decoded or unescaped into a canonical form only once, it is only decoded when encoded data in that form is expected, and that this is done before processing the input further, for example it is not performed after input validation or sanitization. | 1 > 2 |

I read this as "1 > 3" that "One is greater than Three" and we are moving TO Level 1. Did I get that wrong?

But I agree that all injection should be level 1, this is hard core critical issues every app needs to get right.

I would have thought that remote code execution through unsafe deserialization was a quite common problem. It was even in the [OWASP Top 10 2017](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/2017/A8_2017-Insecure_Deserialization) 😄 

For the injections requirements (5.2.11, 5.2.12, 5.3.7, 5.3.10, 5.3.12), the fact that the may be niche is currently not part of the reference criterions in #2690 😄. Some of them are not really really niche I think (LDAP injection for example). CSV injection is arguably more esoteric (?) (and proper injection protection in CSV seems undecidable anyway…).

(Collecting my ideas for further discussion)

What I would like to revisit:
* 5.3.7 - ldap 1 > 3
  * I would like to recommend that LDAP is not used by web application directly. When it is used for authentication, then usually the impact is locking accounts in AD. But, I can not require to not use it.
  * If there is an LDAP injection for whatever reason, the impact is worth L1
  * I would like to come back to L1 or L2 with this
* 5.2.3 imap/smtp
  * not listed by others, but although it is not that widespread solution, the impact of using trusted solution for sending out emails gives high-impact impersionation and phising vectors
  * I would like to move it to L2

What I would like to keep as they are:
* 5.2.12 - memcache 2 > 3
  * the problem is there, but it is not trivial to exploit
  * I prefer L3 over L2
* 5.3.10 - xpath 1 > 3
  * quering from xml - the attack surface is the xml content from where you query, additionally probably can cause denial of service for the parser
  * for sure not L1, I prefer L3 over L2
* 5.5.3 deserialization 1 > 2
  * impact _can_ be big, bit it is not easy to exploit
  * not in the "first priority list", that is why L2

Not so clear cases:
* 5.2.11 - jndi 1 > 3
  * yes, we had log4j, and if we take is away - how often you can year about that?
  * is it L3 because of that? not sure.
* 5.3.12 - latex 2 > 3
  * I assume, that most of those who read this requirement first time have a question "what is latex?" This has been probably one of those requirements that raised the need for "niche" solution
  * I test daily web application security, and I have not seen latex used by web application yet
  * if we only watch impact, then it can be L1
  * if we don't watch the niche argument, then L3 is too much

To conclude that - in certain circumstances many injection type of vulnerabilities may satisfy the condition "if this is the only problem in your application, you have a vulnerability".

Keeping in mind the goal for L1 is "easier entry" and as few requirements we can justify, we can make a difference, what should be in the "first priority" list and what we can leave out.

In big picture, I think we should be quite strict with "syntax layer", e.g. revisit some requirements proposed to be on L3 for potential downgrade.
